{"plan":"1. Approach and rationale
Use a finite-dimensional, multi-start local search on the actual sampled sequence. The core search minimizes a smooth approximation to the maximum over all finite-support correlation lags, using analytic gradients and SLSQP with box bounds and the exact linear mass constraint. Anneal the smoothing parameter, then locally refine a few promising candidates with an epigraph formulation of the original maximum. Project every candidate onto the box-constrained mass hyperplane before scoring or retaining it. Start from the supplied construction when valid, and optionally refine a doubled-resolution version formed by repeating each sample.

This directly addresses the nonconvex, nonsmooth maximum that makes a single gradient run fragile: smoothing supplies useful gradients, multiple seeded starts explore different basins, and epigraph refinement targets the exact metric. The supplied n=45 construction is a valuable feasible fallback and starting point; the 90-sample refinement can explore additional degrees of freedom while remaining small. These are justified algorithmic properties, not evidence that the search will improve the current record. SLSQP is a local method on a generally nonconvex problem; no global-optimality or improvement guarantee is claimed. The authoritative score remains the evaluator’s finite, linear correlation, not the smoothed surrogate.

2. Mathematical specification
For a candidate of runtime length n, let h=(h_0,...,h_{n-1}), dx=2/n, and s=n/2. The feasible set is 0≤h_j≤1 and sum_j h_j=s. For each integer lag k from -(n-1) through n-1, define I_k={i: 0≤i<n and 0≤i+k<n}, q_k(h)=sum_{i in I_k} h_{i+k}(1-h_i), and A_k(h)=dx q_k(h). Then the exact discrete objective is C(h)=max_k A_k(h). This lag convention gives the same full linear-correlation values as np.correlate(h, 1-h, mode='full'); it includes both lag directions and the truncated overlap at each boundary. Do not substitute a circular correlation or an expression that assumes the overlap has full mass.

For j in 0,...,n-1, the analytic derivative is ∂A_k/∂h_j = dx times [sum over i in I_k with i+k=j of (1-h_i), minus sum over i in I_k with i=j of h_{i+k}]. When k=0, both terms apply and yield dx(1-2h_j). These formulas cover all boundary lags without special approximations.

For smoothing parameter η>0 measured in C-score units, use F_η(h)=η log(sum_k exp(A_k(h)/η)). Compute it stably as m+η log(sum_k exp((A_k-m)/η)), where m=max_k A_k. Its gradient is sum_k p_k ∇A_k, with p_k=exp((A_k-m)/η)/sum_l exp((A_l-m)/η). The surrogate obeys C(h)≤F_η(h)≤C(h)+η log(2n-1); only C(h) judges candidates.

The optional exact local refinement introduces t and minimizes t over h and t subject to t-A_k(h)≥0 for every k, sum h_j=s, 0≤h_j≤1, and 0≤t≤1. The t upper bound is valid because each nonnegative q_k is at most sum_j h_j=n/2, so A_k≤1. Each inequality is smooth but generally nonconvex. Its Jacobian row with respect to (h,t) is (-∇A_k,1); the equality Jacobian is (1,...,1,0), and the objective gradient is (0,...,0,1). SLSQP supports these smooth nonlinear constraints but does not make this a convex or globally solved problem. Do not use a convex solver on the original bilinear objective.

The joint feasibility projection for any finite vector v is the Euclidean projection onto {y: 0≤y≤1, sum y=s}. Its KKT form is y_j=clip(v_j-λ,0,1), with the unique λ chosen so sum_j y_j=s. Find λ by bisection: initialize low=min(v)-1 and high=max(v), evaluate the clipped sum at the midpoint, move low upward if that sum exceeds s and otherwise move high downward, and iterate about 70 times. Then correct the remaining floating-point sum residual by adding it to entries with upper-bound slack, or subtracting its magnitude from positive entries, never crossing a bound. Recheck bounds and mass. This joint projection, rather than successive clipping and rescaling, restores both constraints.

3. Implementation procedure
1. Define all helper functions and any callback/exception classes at module top level; do not use closures or lambdas. Use NumPy, time.monotonic, and scipy.optimize.minimize with method SLSQP. Use scipy’s seeded numpy.random.default_rng(seed). Accept run(seed=42, budget_s=1100, **kwargs), and ignore unused keyword arguments safely. Establish a search deadline before optimization, leaving a final reserve as specified in section 5.

2. Read initial_h_values directly from the supplied global when it exists; do not embed, serialize, or reconstruct its entries. Validate that it is a one-dimensional numeric array, has a usable length, contains finite values, and is within [0,1] up to a small numerical tolerance. For an otherwise valid parent, project it to mass s if needed and retain that feasible version and its exact score as the fallback. For the stated n=45 parent, set n0 to its length. If no usable parent exists, use n0=45 and the feasible uniform vector h_j=0.5 as the fallback. If an available parent has length at most 180, it can be searched at that resolution; if its length exceeds 180, preserve it as the fallback and skip the dense local search rather than constructing a large SLSQP problem. Do not mutate the supplied global.

3. Implement a single exact-score helper that checks shape and finiteness, calculates dx=2.0/n, and returns float(max(np.correlate(h, 1-h, mode='full'))*dx). Use this exact helper for every acceptance decision and final score. Implement a lag-data helper that returns the 2n-1 values A_k and, when requested, their gradient matrix of shape (2n-1,n). Enumerate k in increasing order; for k≥0 use i=0,...,n-k-1 and the slices h[k:] and h[:n-k]; for k<0 use i=-k,...,n-1 and the corresponding h[i+k] and h[i] slices. Accumulate the two derivative contributions from section 2 into the appropriate coordinates. Keep this helper consistent with the stated np.correlate lag order.

4. Implement the capped-simplex projection from section 2 as a top-level helper. Reject nonfinite input rather than attempting to repair it. After bisection and residual correction, verify length, finite values, bounds within about 1e-12, and sum within about 1e-10 of n/2. Use np.clip only as part of the KKT projection or a tolerance-level final bound cleanup followed by another mass correction; never clip and rescale sequentially. A failed projection is not a candidate and must not replace the fallback.

5. Maintain a tracker with the best feasible vector and exact score for each resolution and the best candidate across all resolutions. On considering a candidate, project it, recheck feasibility, compute the exact score, and store an independent runtime copy only if it improves the score. If scores tie within 1e-12, prefer the shorter vector. The global-best tracker must always retain the original validated fallback unless a strictly better valid candidate replaces it. A callback should also feed its current iterate to this tracker after projecting it, since an optimizer may stop or time out before returning a usable result.

6. Build reproducible feasible starts at n0. Include the parent or uniform fallback. With a parent, add Gaussian perturbations at scales approximately 0.03, 0.10, and 0.25, using about two starts per scale, and project each perturbed vector. Add about two independent starts made by projecting seeded standard-normal vectors. Without a parent, include uniform plus about seven such projected random starts. Skip duplicates within a small max-norm tolerance. These starts are search heuristics only; feasibility is enforced by projection.

7. For each start, perform smooth continuation with η=(0.02, 0.005, 0.001, 0.0002). At each stage minimize F_η with SLSQP, box bounds [0,1], and the equality sum h=s. Supply the analytic objective gradient, the equality function sum(h)-s, and its all-ones Jacobian. Implement objective, gradient, and constraint helpers at top level and pass their dimensions and η through scipy’s args mechanism. Use ftol around 1e-10 and a default maximum of 100 iterations per stage. Initialize each stage from the preceding stage’s returned vector after projection. Consider both callback iterates and finite solver results for the tracker. A failed or nonfinite solver result must leave the last feasible iterate untouched; it must not erase a better candidate. Catch the explicit deadline-stop exception described below and retain the best candidates collected so far.

8. For exact epigraph refinement, take up to the three best distinct n0 candidates from the smooth searches. Initialize z=(h,t) with feasible projected h and t=min(1,C(h)+1e-8). Minimize t with SLSQP, bounds [0,1] for each h coordinate and [0,1] for t, the mass equality, and the vector inequality with entries t-A_k(h)≥0. Supply the objective, equality, inequality vector, and all Jacobians analytically as given in section 2. Use ftol around 1e-10 and a maximum of 200 iterations. Consider the returned h and callback iterates only after projection and exact rescoring. A solver failure is not fatal: any finite projected candidate may be kept if its exact score improves the tracker, regardless of the solver success flag.

9. If 2n0≤180 and sufficient active time remains, create n1=2n0 from the best n0 vector by repeating every sample twice: h_fine[2i]=h_coarse[i] and h_fine[2i+1]=h_coarse[i]. This exactly doubles the mass and therefore satisfies sum h_fine=n1/2 before any perturbation. Evaluate it with the n1 exact objective and retain it independently. Search n1 from this transfer plus about four projected Gaussian perturbations (scales near 0.03 and 0.10) and one or two projected random starts if time permits. Apply the same smooth continuation and exact epigraph refinement, refining no more than the two best distinct n1 candidates. Do not assume its score equals the coarse score: compare both using their own dx and the exact evaluator formula.

10. The smooth helper computes a stable softmax by subtracting max(A/η), and returns F_η and its weighted analytic gradient. The epigraph constraint helper returns a length-(2n-1) vector and a matrix with one row per lag. All dimensions are computed from the current n. Check the monotonic deadline before starting stages and from the objective/gradient helpers and callback. Define a top-level deadline exception and catch it around each minimize call. A top-level callable callback can save its projected iterate before raising when the deadline is reached. SciPy may return failure status or a partially advanced point; always inspect only finite, correctly shaped vectors and reproject before considering them.

11. Before return, select the best valid tracked vector across resolutions, project it once more, and calculate its exact score afresh. If final validation fails for any reason, return the retained feasible fallback; if no parent was usable, that fallback is the n=45 uniform vector. Return (h_values, c5_bound, n_points), where n_points=len(h_values), and do not return a surrogate score.

4. Search choices and useful variations
The default is n0=45 from the parent, optional n1=90, eight or so n0 starts, four smoothing temperatures (0.02, 0.005, 0.001, 0.0002), at most three coarse epigraph refinements, and at most two fine refinements. Use approximately 100 SLSQP iterations per smooth temperature and 200 for an epigraph refinement. These iteration caps are upper bounds; deadlines take priority.

Programs sampled from this plan may vary the number of perturbation starts (roughly 4–16), Gaussian scales (roughly 0.02–0.35), final η (roughly 0.0001–0.001), or whether to spend remaining time on n1. Vary these reproducibly through seed and explicit parameters. A reasonable adaptation is to use fewer starts when the active budget is short, and to enable n1 only after at least one valid coarse candidate has been retained. Do not alter the exact objective, finite-lag boundaries, mass constraint, projection, or exact-score acceptance rule. Every experimental candidate remains subject to those correctness requirements.

5. Compute budget and robustness
All cost estimates here are unmeasured. Building lag values and analytic gradients costs O(n^2) arithmetic and O(n^2) storage when the full gradient matrix is used. At the intended n=45 and n=90, that is at most 179 by 90 gradient entries per evaluation at the fine resolution. SLSQP’s dense constrained subproblems, especially the epigraph refinement, can cost more than forming lag data; cap the searched resolutions at 180 and limit epigraph refinements. Do not construct a large n-by-n-by-lag tensor or use a dense quadratic-program formulation of all bilinear terms.

Let start=time.monotonic(). Reserve reserve=max(2 seconds, min(20 seconds, 0.03*max(budget_s,0))) for final validation and return, and set the hard search deadline to start+max(0,budget_s-reserve). Within that active time, aim to spend about 55% on n0 starts and smooth continuation, up to 30% on n1 if eligible, and the remainder on epigraph refinements or more starts. Treat these as adaptive targets, not a reason to overrun: callbacks and helper checks must stop work at the relevant deadline, and every phase checks time before launching another SLSQP call. If a phase ends early, spend its unused time on the best candidates or starts at the current resolution. If budget_s is very small, do no optimization and return the already validated fallback.

The best feasible candidate is stored before any search. Numerical overflow in exponentials is prevented by stable log-sum-exp; nonfinite values, invalid shapes, failed projections, and infeasible solver points are discarded. If SLSQP reports failure, keep valid callback or returned candidates that pass projection and exact rescoring, and otherwise continue from the previous feasible start. Reserve time so timeout handling and final scoring can complete. No timing or score improvement is assumed.

6. Validation and return contract
For every retained and returned vector, check one-dimensional shape, expected n, finite values, 0≤h_j≤1, and abs(sum(h)-n/2)≤1e-10 (or a suitably tight floating-point tolerance). Recompute c5_bound from the exact full np.correlate expression with dx=2.0/n; do not use the smooth objective or an epigraph t as the returned value. If the scaffold’s evaluate_erdos_solution helper has a known callable interface, it may additionally be used to cross-check this result, but the explicit formula in the task is sufficient and must remain authoritative.

Include small implementation sanity checks, not claims that they have already been run: for short deterministic vectors, compare the helper’s ordered lag values with np.correlate(...)*dx; check that the maximum agrees with the exact-score helper; and finite-difference-check the analytic lag or smooth gradient on a small interior vector. Check the projection on random and perturbed vectors for bounds and mass, including fractional targets for odd n. Finally verify that the selected candidate is rescored after projection and that its returned n_points matches its length."}

plan.description: The complete, detailed, self-contained implementation specification, with all six numbered sections.
